BEFORE THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
                             OF THE STATE OF MISSOURI

    In the Matter of Union Electric Company           §
    d/b/a Ameren Missouri's Tariffs to Adjust Its     §               No. ER-2026-0291
                                                      §
    Revenues for Electric Service                     §

           SIERRA CLUB’S REPLY TO AMEREN MISSOURI’S RESPONSE TO OTHER
         PARTIES’ FILINGS SEEKING ADDITIONAL LOCAL PUBLIC HEARINGS

          Sierra Club, pursuant to 20 CSR 4240-2.080(13), files this reply to a filing made by Union

Electric Company d/b/a Ameren Missouri (“Ameren”), to reiterate its requests that the

Commission grant the Consumers Council of Missouri’s Motion for Additional Local Public

Hearing in the City of St. Louis.1


          Ameren’s response fails to address any of the reasons to grant an additional local public

hearing that Sierra Club provided in its 10/19/2026 Response.2 To grant the hearings, the

Commission need only find that an additional local public hearing would be beneficial. Sierra Club

therefore respectfully requests that it do so and locate the hearing in North St. Louis, due to its

current struggles with energy burdens and tornado recovery, which may soon be compounded by

the double-digit rate increases proposed by Ameren in this case.




1
 Motion for Additional Public Hearing in the City of St. Louis, Consumers Council of Missouri (Filed
10/16/2026), In the Matter of Union Electric Company d/b/a Ameren Missouri’s Tariffs to Adjust its
Revenues for Electric Service, MO PSC Case No. ER-2026-0291, EFIS Item No. 58.
2
 Sierra Club’s Response in Support of Consumers Council of Missouri’s Motion for Additional Local
Public Hearings in the City of St. Louis (Filed 10/19/2026), In the Matter of Union Electric Company d/b/a
Ameren Missouri’s Tariff to Adjust Its Revenues for Electric Service, MO PSC Case No. ER-2026-0291,
EFIS Item No. 59.
     1. Ameren’s Response Invents Requirements Unsupported by Law
        Ameren first argues that the Commission must provide a consistent number of public

hearings in each of its rate cases, unless the service area at issue changes significantly in size.3 But

no law or regulation requires the Commission to provide the same or a similar number of public

hearings in each rate case. Quite the opposite—the Commission has broad discretionary authority

to “set the time and place for all hearings,” and therefore is not bound to provide the same number

of public hearings in each subsequent rate case. See Mo. Code Regs. Ann. 20, § 4240-2.110(1).

This wide discretion conflicts with Ameren’s asserted rule because it would limit the

Commission’s decisions to past practices.


        Ameren’s second argument amounts to a requirement that intervenors must “present . . .

compelling logic” or evidence “supporting the conclusion that the public will not have a fair

opportunity to participate” in the public hearing process.4 Neither of these are requirements under

Missouri law. Under § 4240-2.110, there is no burden of proof placed on any party, and there are

no factors that must be present for the Commission to grant an additional local public hearing. It

is an entirely discretionary decision, not one demanding any specific showing.


        The Commission wields a broad, flexible power to grant additional local public hearings

in communities that are directly or uniquely affected by utility activities, and has done so before.

In 2018, when the Empire District Electric Company applied for approval to develop wind

 generation, the City of Joplin requested a local public hearing, and the Commission granted it

despite Empire’s and Staff’s complaints that “holding a local public hearing regarding this type of

application is not required and highly unusual.”5 This was because of the unique impact of

Empire’s operations on rates and stranded costs in Joplin.6 The Commission was empowered to

grant the hearing because it would be “beneficial to receive comments from Missouri ratepayers

who could be affected by Empire’s proposed plan.”7 The Commission should be similarly satisfied

in this case that grossly disproportionate energy burdens, abandoned tornado recovery efforts, and

sharply rising electricity rates at least justify a public hearing that North City residents will not

have to find an internet connection or transportation to participate in.


           Finally, Ameren argued that intervenors have “presented no evidence that supports the

conclusion that it is necessary or proper to increase the number of in-person local public hearings

by 40%,” and therefore the request should be denied.8 Although it provided no citation, Ameren is

likely referring to Mo. Ann. Stat. § 386.040, which establishes the PSC, and vests it not only with

all the enumerated powers of the chapter, but also “all powers necessary or proper to enable it to

carry out fully and effectually all the purposes of this chapter.” But the Missouri Supreme Court

 has read this provision as an expansion, not a limitation on the Commission’s power.9 Therefore,

the PSC certainly has discretion to grant an additional local public hearing under this provision.


        In sum, there is no requirement that the Commission maintain consistent numbers of local

public hearings year-over-year, no requirement that intervenors prove denial of fair opportunity to

be heard, and no requirement that intervenors prove that an additional local public hearing is

“necessary or proper.” All the Commission must find to grant an additional local public hearing is

that doing so is “beneficial.”10


     2. An Additional Local Public Hearing in North St. Louis is Beneficial, Fair, and Important
        An additional local public hearing in North St. Louis is beneficial for two reasons. First,

North City residents have three acute concerns with Ameren: energy burdens, connection problems

relating to failed tornado recovery, and rising rates. Second, North St. Louis residents, on average,

are less equipped to utilize the alternative hearing options stressed by Ameren’s response,11 like

different locations or virtual hearings.


        Many tornado survivors in North St Louis are going into their second winter with

sustained tornado damage, compromising weatherization efforts. Only 59 repair projects out of

context generally is understood in American law to mean something closer to “useful” or “helpful.” See
McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. 316, 345-50 (1819).

 2,674 applications have been completed thus far. 12This is concerning because hypothermia can set

in at 40 F, and even indoor temperatures as high as 60-65 F can lead to hypothermia in older

adults.13 In addition to existing high energy burden and home repair costs, many tornado-impacted

residents could have an increased risk of temperature-related health hazards if their utilities get

disconnected due to unaffordability.14 Therefore, the tornado-impacted communities of North St

Louis City should have more input on potentially increased utility rates, not less.


          Local public hearings are the best way for communities to express their frustrations with

energy burdens, yet Ameren's response dismisses the problem as one of the same old “issues CCM

routinely cites.” While Ameren may tire of hearing about it does not mean that the grossly

disproportionate energy burdens borne by North St. Louis residents have disappeared.15


          Local public hearings give customers who often lack legal representation or the free time

to file EFIS submissions, the chance to share their real-world experience and the way they are

impacted by Ameren’s activities. In the PSC context, this testimony can be quite effective: in a

2012 rate case, the Commission rejected a residential rate increase due to “economic woes, on

          North City residents are also less likely to be able to utilize the alternative hearing options

touted by Ameren. North City residents face transportation barriers that require many to spend

hours riding public transport to and from work.18 Many also lack stable internet service: only 48%

of households in North City have broadband internet access necessary for a virtual hearing.19 For

a hearing to be meaningful, it must be tailored to the “capacities and circumstances of those who

           Ameren offers no response to these facts, other than the conclusory statement that to grant

an additional hearing in North City “would reflect bad policy.”21 Ameren is mistaken. A

Commission that responds to rather than ignores local needs reflects good policy, and Sierra Club

therefore reiterates its request that the Commission grant the Consumers Council of Missouri’s

Motion for Additional Local Public Hearing in the City of St. Louis,22 and further requests that

this additional hearing be held in the North side of the City of St. Louis, such as at the O’Fallon

Park Rec Complex.23
